title: The Introduction
paragraphs: Nature (the art by which God has made and governs the world) is imitated by the art of man in many things, and in this one too: that human art can make an Artificial Animal. For since life is but a motion of limbs, beginning in some principal part within, why may we not say that all Automata (engines that move themselves by springs and wheels, as a watch does) have an artificial life? For what is the heart but a spring; the nerves but so many strings; the joints but so many wheels, giving motion to the whole body just as the maker intended? Art goes further still, imitating that rational and most excellent work of Nature, Man. For by art is created that great LEVIATHAN called a COMMON-WEALTH, or STATE (in Latin CIVITAS), which is but an Artificial Man, though of greater stature and strength than the natural one, for whose protection and defence it was intended. In it, the Sovereignty is an Artificial Soul, giving life and motion to the whole body; the magistrates and other officers of judicature and execution are artificial joints; reward and punishment (by which, fastened to the seat of the Sovereignty, every joint and member is moved to perform its duty) are the nerves that do the same in the natural body; the wealth and riches of all the particular members are the strength; Salus Populi (the people's safety) is its business; counsellors, by whom all things needful for it to know are suggested to it, are the memory; equity and laws are an artificial reason and will; concord is its health; sedition its sickness; and civil war its death. Lastly, the pacts and covenants by which the parts of this Body Politic were at first made, set together, and united resemble that Fiat, or the Let Us Make Man, pronounced by God in the Creation.
First, the matter of it, and the maker, both of which is Man.
Secondly, how and by what covenants it is made; what the rights and just power or authority of a Sovereign are; and what preserves it and dissolves it.

Concerning the first, there is a saying much abused of late, that wisdom is acquired not by reading books but by reading men. As a consequence, those persons who for the most part can give no other proof of being wise take great delight in showing what they think they have read in men, by uncharitable censures of one another behind their backs. But there is another saying, not understood of late, by which they might learn truly to read one another, if they would take the pains; and that is, Nosce Teipsum, Read Thy Self. This was not meant, as it is now used, to countenance either the barbarous behaviour of men in power towards their inferiors, or to encourage men of low degree to a saucy behaviour towards their betters. Rather, it was meant to teach us that, because of the similarity between the thoughts and passions of one man and the thoughts and passions of another, whoever looks into himself and considers what he does when he thinks, opines, reasons, hopes, fears, etc., and on what grounds, will thereby read and know what the thoughts and passions of all other men are, on similar occasions. I mean the similarity of the passions, which are the same in all men—desire, fear, hope, etc.—not the similarity of the objects of the passions, which are the things desired, feared, hoped for, etc. For these the individual constitution and particular education make vary so widely, and they are so easily kept hidden from us, that the characters of a man's heart, blotted and confounded as they are by dissembling, lying, counterfeiting, and erroneous doctrines, are legible only to Him who searches hearts. And although by men's actions we sometimes discover their designs, yet to do this without comparing them with our own, and distinguishing all the circumstances by which the case may come to be altered, is to decipher without a key, and to be for the most part deceived, by too much trust or by too much diffidence, depending on whether the reader himself is a good or an evil man.

But let one man read another by his actions ever so perfectly, it serves him only with his acquaintances, who are but few. He that is to govern a whole nation must read in himself not this or that particular man, but Mankind. That is hard to do—harder than learning any language or science. Yet when I have set down my own reading orderly and clearly, the pains left to another will only be to consider whether he does not find the same in himself. For this kind of doctrine admits of no other demonstration.
